the idea of your bitcoin or crypto resting easy in some secret location while you enjoy life not worrying about it is currently unrealistic

it was somewhat realistic before. but the cost of cybersecurity attacks went down exponentially, and continues to go down exponentially on a monthly basis as new, more capable AI models are publicly released

what this means is that your cybersecurity must now be actively managed. it cannot be passive. someone must worry about your shit every day and every night, actively dismiss old assumptions and attempt new approaches on a weekly basis to adapt to a dynamic landscape of new threats

so your options are:

1. be the one who is worried. assess developing threats yourself on a daily/weekly basis, stay up to date with new models and tools as soon as they’re launched, analyze your own security practices ruthlessly day and night. for most people, including most experts, i think this is highly impractical. but you’re welcome to try

2. store your coins with a competent third party service that you trust to do the worrying for you. they should have the resources, skills and incentives to actively manage the cybersecurity risk for you. if you don’t want to worry yourself you need to pay someone else to be worried. it is what it is

i’m not trying to shit on self-custody. technically you can have someone professional actively worry about your self-custody setup, that’s fine too

one day, the threat level will plateau and will stop increasing exponentially on a monthly basis, and then passive security will gradually become acceptable. but today is not that day

If you're going to survive in crypto, you have to accept what it actually is.

You're going to get 35% pullbacks. You'll get 50% drawdowns.

None of it matters if you understand what you own.

The core of what you hold should be a small handful of networks with real, provable long-term value and genuine adoption. Get that right, and the drawdowns stop being terrifying. They become the point.

Because this is a long game. I think these networks become the pension for an entire generation. You don't trade your way there. You build a thesis, you accumulate, you keep something back for the big sell-offs, and you let time and adoption do the work.

The volatility is the price of admission. The people who make it are the ones who stop flinching at it.

That's what I've written up this week. The whole picture, thirteen years on.

Basically the r/r for holding STRC at $100 is atrocious if we know they will always hit the ATM at $100, because you get all the downside volatility and only 1% yield every month as upside. Given the type of volatility STRC has (10% swings), if you short it at $100, you're almost certain that you'll get out in profit on its next drawdown.

Strategy claims that they target a 1% range at $99-$100, but that's physically impossible, because even if the dividend rate is variable in theory, in the short-term the div rate is fixed, meaning it will have a similar volatility profile as STRF, ie at least 10% swings.
If you cap the upside at $100, the 10% swings will be capped at $100 and you mechanically decrease the bottom of these volatile moves. I think it's much more realistic to target a $95-$105 range, because the average price of STRC would then be around $100 (which is the goal). In the current situation, by trying to be cute and "guarantee that STRC won't top $100", Strategy forces the whole thing to trade in a $90-$100 range (at best), meaning the average price of STRC is significantly below $100.

What I foresee is gigantic biological data factories: millions of standard lab machines, operated 24/7 by autonomous humanoid robots, with agents designing the next experiments in real time.

Every variable is captured: temperature, protocol, machine, reagent, timing, outcome, failure. Petabytes of clean, structured, verifiable data continuously flowing back into the models.

I call it bounded serendipity: creating a controlled space where AI can explore millions of experiments, encounter the unexpected, verify what works, and turn the physical world into both training data and scientific discovery.
